# =============================================================================
# TESTS FOR: FIRST MODEL: FACTOR: SPECIFICITY   (version 4)
# =============================================================================
# The model itself lives in first_model_factor_specificity.py; this file only
# tests it. Every case uses FAKE primers and a FAKE target built by hand, so
# each expected answer is worked out on paper first ("Cases solvable by hand"
# in the proposal). journal/test_cases_specificity.txt lists every case.
#
# Run it with:  python3 journal/test_first_model_factor_specificity.py
# =============================================================================

import random

from first_model_factor_specificity import (
    compare_site, print_report, reverse_complement, run_model, MIN_KNOWN_BASES,
)


# =============================================================================
# SECTION 1: FAKE PRIMERS AND FAKE TARGET BUILDING BLOCKS
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Every fake primer and probe is 18-30 bases long, the range of real qPCR
# oligos (the CDC primers and probes are 18-24 bases).
#
#   Set A (used by most cases): 20-base forward, 24-base reverse, 26-base probe
#   Set B (length-limit cases): 18-base forward, 30-base reverse
#   plus an 18-base palindrome (Case 14) and a 20-base overlapping reverse
#   primer (Case 12)
#
# The fake target is assembled from pieces of known length, so every expected
# position and product size below can be added up by hand.
#
# Filler is poly-A: no primer contains AAAAA or TTTTT, so the filler cannot
# match any 5-base seed and never creates accidental binding sites.
# =============================================================================

# -- Set A: 20 + 26 + 24 = 70 bp amplicon
FORWARD_A = "ACGGTCTAGCATTGCAGTCC"                  # 20 bases
REVERSE_A = "TCCGATAGTCAGCTTGGACAGTCA"              # 24 bases
REVERSE_SITE_A = reverse_complement(REVERSE_A)      # "TGACTGTCCAAGCTGACTATCGGA"
INSERT_A = "CGTACGTTGCATGCCTAGGTGATCAG"             # 26 bases between the sites
PROBE_A = INSERT_A                                  # the probe binds the whole insert

# -- Set B: 18 + 25 + 30 = 73 bp amplicon
FORWARD_B = "CAGTGCTTACGGATCGAG"                    # 18 bases
REVERSE_B = "GTCATCGACTGTAGCTTCGAGACGTTAGCC"        # 30 bases
REVERSE_SITE_B = reverse_complement(REVERSE_B)      # "GGCTAACGTCTCGAAGCTACAGTCGATGAC"
INSERT_B = "TGACCGTATCAGGTCATGCAGTCCA"              # 25 bases between the sites


def filler(n):
    """n bases of background sequence that no primer can bind."""
    return "A" * n


def amplicon():
    """Set A: forward site + insert + reverse site = 20 + 26 + 24 = 70 bp product.

    Amplicon offsets (0-based): forward site 0-19, insert 20-45, reverse site 46-69.
    """
    return FORWARD_A + INSERT_A + REVERSE_SITE_A


def amplicon_b():
    """Set B: forward site + insert + reverse site = 18 + 25 + 30 = 73 bp product.

    Amplicon offsets (0-based): forward site 0-17, insert 18-42, reverse site 43-72.
    """
    return FORWARD_B + INSERT_B + REVERSE_SITE_B


def mutate(seq, offset, new_base):
    """Return seq with the base at offset replaced (used to plant mismatches or Ns)."""
    return seq[:offset] + new_base + seq[offset + 1:]


def change_base(seq, offset):
    """Plant a guaranteed mismatch: A becomes C, anything else becomes A."""
    return mutate(seq, offset, "C" if seq[offset] == "A" else "A")


# =============================================================================
# SECTION 2: CASES SOLVABLE BY HAND: CORE (version 1)
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Each case states its expected answer (worked out on paper), runs the model,
# and checks the model agrees. A failed check stops the program.
# Positions in the checks are 0-based (as stored); the report prints 1-based.
# =============================================================================

def check(condition, message):
    if not condition:
        raise AssertionError(message)
    print(f"  PASS: {message}")


def product_lengths(result):
    """Lengths of the products whose status is 'product', smallest first."""
    return sorted(p["length"] for p in result["products"] if p["status"] == "product")


def site_of(result, primer):
    """The first site found for one primer."""
    return [s for s in result["sites"] if s["primer"] == primer][0]


# -- Case 1: exact match, one product ----------------------------------------
# a) Set A. target = 10 filler + 70 bp amplicon + 10 filler
#    forward binds "+" at 10..30, reverse binds "-" at 56..80, product 10..80 = 70 bp
# b) Set B, primers of 18 and 30 bases. Same layout:
#    forward "+" at 10..28, reverse "-" at 53..83, product 10..83 = 73 bp
def case_exact_match():
    target = filler(10) + amplicon() + filler(10)
    result = run_model(FORWARD_A, REVERSE_A, target, max_mismatches=0)
    print_report("Case 1a: exact match, set A", result)
    check(product_lengths(result) == [70], "exactly one product, 70 bp (20 + 26 + 24)")
    product = result["products"][0]
    check((product["start"], product["end"]) == (10, 80), "product spans 10-80 (printed 11-80)")

    target = filler(10) + amplicon_b() + filler(10)
    result = run_model(FORWARD_B, REVERSE_B, target, max_mismatches=0)
    print_report("Case 1b: exact match, set B (18- and 30-base primers)", result)
    check(product_lengths(result) == [73], "exactly one product, 73 bp (18 + 25 + 30)")
    product = result["products"][0]
    check((product["start"], product["end"]) == (10, 83), "product spans 10-83 (printed 11-83)")


# -- Case 2: reverse-strand matches ------------------------------------------
# Reverse-complement the whole Case 1a target. The product is the same 70 bp,
# but now the REVERSE primer is the "+" site and the FORWARD primer is "-".
def case_reverse_strand():
    target = reverse_complement(filler(10) + amplicon() + filler(10))
    result = run_model(FORWARD_A, REVERSE_A, target, max_mismatches=0)
    print_report("Case 2: whole target on the other strand", result)
    check(product_lengths(result) == [70], "exactly one product, still 70 bp")
    check(result["products"][0]["left"]["primer"] == "reverse", "reverse primer is now the '+' site")
    check(result["products"][0]["right"]["primer"] == "forward", "forward primer is now the '-' site")


# -- Case 3: introduced mismatches at the 3' end -----------------------------
# Forward site: last base (amplicon offset 19) C -> G, distance 1 from 3' end.
# Reverse site: first plus-strand base (amplicon offset 46) T -> C. The reverse
# primer's 3' end is the LEFT end of a "-" site, so this is also distance 1.
# In the reverse primer's own direction: its 3' base A now faces genome G
# (the complement of plus-strand C).
# Severity: the forward primer's C sits opposite template C (complement of
# genome G): C-C is SEVERE. The reverse primer's A sits opposite template C
# (complement of genome G): A-C is MILD.
def case_mismatches():
    seq = mutate(mutate(amplicon(), 19, "G"), 46, "C")
    target = filler(10) + seq + filler(10)

    result = run_model(FORWARD_A, REVERSE_A, target, max_mismatches=0)
    print_report("Case 3a: mismatches, tolerance 0", result)
    check(product_lengths(result) == [], "no product when no mismatches are allowed")
    check(result["outcomes"]["forward"] == "mismatched", "forward is 'mismatched'")
    check(result["assay"] == "no product", "assay is 'no product'")
    check(result["near_misses"]["forward"]["changes"] ==
          [{"from_3prime": 1, "primer": "C", "genome": "G", "severity": "severe"}],
          "forward near-miss: 1 from 3' end, primer C, genome G, severe")
    check(result["near_misses"]["reverse"]["changes"] ==
          [{"from_3prime": 1, "primer": "A", "genome": "G", "severity": "mild"}],
          "reverse near-miss: 1 from 3' end, primer A, genome G, mild")

    result = run_model(FORWARD_A, REVERSE_A, target, max_mismatches=1)
    print_report("Case 3b: mismatches, tolerance 1", result)
    check(product_lengths(result) == [70], "one product when 1 mismatch is allowed")
    check(result["products"][0]["left"]["mismatch_from_3prime"] == [1],
          "forward mismatch reported at the 3'-terminal base")
    check(result["products"][0]["right"]["mismatch_from_3prime"] == [1],
          "reverse mismatch reported at the 3'-terminal base")
    check(result["products"][0]["left"]["three_prime_risk"] == "high", "forward site: 3' risk HIGH (severe C-C)")
    check(result["products"][0]["right"]["three_prime_risk"] == "low", "reverse site: 3' risk LOW (mild A-C)")
    check(result["products"][0]["three_prime_risk"] == "high", "product takes the worse grade: HIGH")
    check(len(result["warnings"]) == 1, "one 3' risk warning is printed")


# -- Case 3c: mismatch far from the 3' end -----------------------------------
# Change the forward site's FIRST base (offset 0) A -> G: distance 20 from the
# 3' end. Primer A opposite template C (complement of genome G): A-C, mild.
def case_mismatch_5prime():
    target = filler(10) + mutate(amplicon(), 0, "G") + filler(10)
    result = run_model(FORWARD_A, REVERSE_A, target, max_mismatches=1)
    print_report("Case 3c: mismatch at the 5' end", result)
    check(result["products"][0]["left"]["changes"] ==
          [{"from_3prime": 20, "primer": "A", "genome": "G", "severity": "mild"}],
          "forward mismatch 20 from 3' end: primer A, genome G, mild (A-C)")
    check(result["products"][0]["three_prime_risk"] is None, "a 5' mismatch gives no 3' risk")


# -- Case 4: multiple products -----------------------------------------------
# Two copies of the amplicon: 10 filler + amplicon + 30 filler + amplicon + 10.
# Copy 1 at 10..80, copy 2 at 110..180. Products with max_length=1000:
#   copy1 F x copy1 R = 70 bp, copy2 F x copy2 R = 70 bp,
#   copy1 F x copy2 R = 180 - 10 = 170 bp  (the long "outer" product)
# copy2 F x copy1 R faces away -> no product.
def case_multiple_products():
    target = filler(10) + amplicon() + filler(30) + amplicon() + filler(10)
    result = run_model(FORWARD_A, REVERSE_A, target, max_mismatches=0)
    print_report("Case 4: two copies of the target", result)
    check(len(result["sites"]) == 4, "4 binding sites (2 forward, 2 reverse)")
    check(product_lengths(result) == [70, 70, 170], "products of 70, 70 and 170 bp")

    result = run_model(FORWARD_A, REVERSE_A, target, max_mismatches=0, max_length=100)
    print_report("Case 4b: same, max product length 100", result)
    check(product_lengths(result) == [70, 70], "the 170 bp product is dropped when the limit is 100")


# -- Case 5: primers facing away from each other -----------------------------
# Put the reverse site FIRST and the forward site after it:
# they point away from each other, so nothing is amplified.
def case_facing_away():
    target = filler(10) + REVERSE_SITE_A + INSERT_A + FORWARD_A + filler(10)
    result = run_model(FORWARD_A, REVERSE_A, target, max_mismatches=0)
    print_report("Case 5: primers facing away", result)
    check(len(result["sites"]) == 2, "both primers still bind")
    check(result["assay"] == "no product", "but no product forms")


# -- Case 6: no binding site at all ------------------------------------------
def case_no_site():
    result = run_model(FORWARD_A, REVERSE_A, filler(200), max_mismatches=2)
    print_report("Case 6: target without the primer sites", result)
    check(len(result["sites"]) == 0, "no sites")
    check(result["assay"] == "no product", "assay is 'no product'")
    check(result["near_misses"]["forward"] is None, "no near-miss either: nothing is close")


# =============================================================================
# SECTION 3: CASES SOLVABLE BY HAND: BAD SEQUENCING DATA (version 2)
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Each case imitates a trace that poor sequencing leaves in a finished genome
# and checks the model says "not assessable" instead of "mismatched".
# =============================================================================

# -- Case 7: Ns inside a primer site -----------------------------------------
# Replace amplicon offsets 5 and 6 (inside the forward site) with N.
# On the "+" strand, offset 5 is 20-5 = 15 and offset 6 is 20-6 = 14 bases
# from the 3' end. With tolerance 0 the Ns must NOT count as mismatches.
def case_n_in_site():
    seq = mutate(mutate(amplicon(), 5, "N"), 6, "N")
    target = filler(10) + seq + filler(10)
    result = run_model(FORWARD_A, REVERSE_A, target, max_mismatches=0)
    print_report("Case 7: Ns inside the forward site", result)
    forward_site = site_of(result, "forward")
    check(forward_site["mismatches"] == 0, "Ns are not counted as mismatches")
    check(forward_site["unknown_from_3prime"] == [14, 15], "Ns reported 14 and 15 bases from the 3' end")
    check(result["outcomes"]["forward"] == "not assessable", "forward is 'not assessable'")
    check(result["outcomes"]["reverse"] == "binds", "reverse still binds")
    check(result["assay"] == "not assessable", "assay is 'not assessable'")


# -- Case 7b: same Ns, but 2 mismatches allowed (version 4) ------------------
# 0 real mismatches + 2 unknown bases = 2, which still fits an allowance of 2:
# even if both Ns were mismatches the primer would bind, so the missing data
# cannot change the answer. The site is "binds", not "not assessable".
def case_n_cannot_change_answer():
    seq = mutate(mutate(amplicon(), 5, "N"), 6, "N")
    target = filler(10) + seq + filler(10)
    result = run_model(FORWARD_A, REVERSE_A, target, max_mismatches=2)
    print_report("Case 7b: Ns inside the forward site, tolerance 2", result)
    check(site_of(result, "forward")["outcome"] == "binds", "forward binds: the Ns cannot change the answer")
    check(result["assay"] == "product", "assay is 'product'")


# -- Case 8: sequence ends partway through a primer site ---------------------
# target = 10 filler + forward site + insert + first 12 bases of the reverse
# site. The reverse site would span 56..80 but the sequence stops at 68, so
# 12 of its 24 bases are present (>= 10 required) and all of them match.
def case_truncated_end():
    target = filler(10) + FORWARD_A + INSERT_A + REVERSE_SITE_A[:12]
    result = run_model(FORWARD_A, REVERSE_A, target, max_mismatches=0)
    print_report("Case 8: sequence stops inside the reverse site", result)
    check(site_of(result, "reverse")["start"] == 56, "reverse site would span 56-80")
    check(site_of(result, "reverse")["reason"] == "runs off the end of the sequence",
          "reason is 'runs off the end'")
    check(result["outcomes"]["reverse"] == "not assessable", "reverse is 'not assessable'")
    check(result["assay"] == "not assessable", "assay is 'not assessable'")


# -- Case 9: sequence starts partway through a primer site -------------------
# Drop the first 4 bases of the amplicon: 16 of the forward site's 20 bases
# remain at the very start of the sequence, so it "runs off the start".
def case_truncated_start():
    target = amplicon()[4:] + filler(10)
    result = run_model(FORWARD_A, REVERSE_A, target, max_mismatches=0)
    print_report("Case 9: sequence starts inside the forward site", result)
    forward_site = site_of(result, "forward")
    check(forward_site["start"] == -4, "forward site would have started 4 bases before the sequence")
    check(forward_site["reason"] == "runs off the start of the sequence", "reason is 'runs off the start'")
    check(result["assay"] == "not assessable", "assay is 'not assessable'")


# -- Case 10: real mismatches next to missing data ---------------------------
# Four real mismatches in the reverse site (amplicon offsets 50, 55, 60, 65 =
# site offsets 4, 9, 14, 19) plus an N in the forward site (offset 3).
# Tolerance 1: the reverse primer has more real differences than allowed, so
# it is "mismatched". Because the reverse primer cannot bind anywhere, no
# product is possible whatever the N hides: the assay is "no product", NOT
# "not assessable" (fixed in version 3).
# The 4 mismatches, 5 bases apart, cut the 24-base reverse site into five
# stretches of 4 bases, so the near-miss search (which needs an exact 5-base
# stretch) reports "none close". This shows that limit honestly.
# Version 4: the forward site has 0 mismatches + 1 N, which fits an allowance
# of 1 even if the N is a mismatch, so the forward primer "binds".
def case_mismatched_beats_unknown():
    seq = amplicon()
    for offset in (50, 55, 60, 65):
        seq = change_base(seq, offset)
    seq = mutate(seq, 3, "N")
    target = filler(10) + seq + filler(10)
    result = run_model(FORWARD_A, REVERSE_A, target, max_mismatches=1)
    print_report("Case 10: reverse truly mismatched, N elsewhere", result)
    check(result["outcomes"]["reverse"] == "mismatched", "reverse is 'mismatched'")
    check(result["outcomes"]["forward"] == "binds", "forward binds: 1 N fits an allowance of 1")
    check(result["assay"] == "no product", "assay is 'no product': the reverse primer cannot bind")
    check(result["near_misses"]["reverse"] is None,
          "near-miss not found: no exact 5-base stretch left (known limit)")


# =============================================================================
# SECTION 4: CASES SOLVABLE BY HAND: EDGE CASES (version 3)
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Situations the earlier cases did not cover.
# =============================================================================

# -- Case 11: a primer pairs with itself -------------------------------------
# Put the forward primer's reverse complement where the reverse site would be.
# The forward primer now binds "+" at 10..30 AND "-" at 56..76, so it makes a
# 20 + 26 + 20 = 66 bp product on its own; the reverse primer binds nowhere.
def case_self_pairing():
    target = filler(10) + FORWARD_A + INSERT_A + reverse_complement(FORWARD_A) + filler(10)
    result = run_model(FORWARD_A, REVERSE_A, target, max_mismatches=0)
    print_report("Case 11: forward primer pairs with itself", result)
    product = result["products"][0]
    check((product["left"]["primer"], product["right"]["primer"]) == ("forward", "forward"),
          "the product is forward x forward")
    check(product_lengths(result) == [66], "it is 66 bp")
    check(result["outcomes"]["reverse"] == "mismatched", "the reverse primer does not bind")


# -- Case 12: overlapping primer sites ---------------------------------------
# A 20-base reverse primer whose site starts INSIDE the forward site:
# site = last 5 bases of the forward site + first 15 bases of the insert.
# Forward site 10..30, overlapping reverse site 25..45 -> product 10..45 = 35 bp.
OVERLAP_REVERSE = reverse_complement(FORWARD_A[-5:] + INSERT_A[:15])


def case_overlapping_sites():
    target = filler(10) + FORWARD_A + INSERT_A[:15] + filler(10)
    result = run_model(FORWARD_A, OVERLAP_REVERSE, target, max_mismatches=0)
    print_report("Case 12: primer sites overlap by 5 bases", result)
    check(site_of(result, "reverse")["start"] == 25, "reverse site starts at 25, inside the forward site")
    check(product_lengths(result) == [35], "one 35 bp product")


# -- Case 13: mismatch allowance too high for the primer length --------------
# 3 mismatches -> 4 pieces. The 30-base reverse primer gives 30 // 4 = 7-base
# pieces (fine), but the 18-base forward primer gives 18 // 4 = 4-base pieces,
# shorter than k = 5, so the search cannot guarantee it finds every site.
# It must stop with an error that names the forward primer.
def case_allowance_too_high():
    print("\n--- Case 13: 3 mismatches allowed on an 18-base primer ---")
    try:
        run_model(FORWARD_B, REVERSE_B, amplicon_b(), max_mismatches=3)
        check(False, "an error is raised")
    except ValueError as error:
        print(f"  error message: {error}")
        check(str(error).startswith("forward: 18 bases"),
              "an error names the 18-base forward primer instead of a silently incomplete search")


# -- Case 14: palindromic primer binds both strands at the same spot ---------
# GACTAGCTTAAGCTAGTC (18 bases) is its own reverse complement, so ONE place in
# the target is a "+" site and a "-" site at once (both 10..28). The two sites
# face each other, but the "product" would be only 18 bp (< 20 minimum).
PALINDROME = "GACTAGCTTAAGCTAGTC"


def case_palindrome():
    target = filler(10) + PALINDROME + filler(10)
    result = run_model(PALINDROME, REVERSE_A, target, max_mismatches=0)
    print_report("Case 14: palindromic primer", result)
    strands = sorted((s["strand"], s["start"]) for s in result["sites"] if s["primer"] == "forward")
    check(strands == [("+", 10), ("-", 10)], "same spot found on both strands")
    check(result["assay"] == "no product", "no product (18 bp is below the 20 bp minimum)")


# -- Case 15: degenerate base in the primer ----------------------------------
# Forward primer with Y (= C or T) at offset 9: ACGGTCTAGYATTGCAGTCC.
# Genome C or T at that spot -> 0 mismatches. Genome A -> 1 mismatch,
# 20 - 9 = 11 bases from the 3' end, reported as "primer Y, genome A".
# Severity: template T faces primer C or T (C-T, T-T): neither is severe -> mild.
DEGENERATE_FORWARD = mutate(FORWARD_A, 9, "Y")


def case_degenerate_primer():
    for genome_base in ("C", "T"):
        target = filler(10) + mutate(amplicon(), 9, genome_base) + filler(10)
        result = run_model(DEGENERATE_FORWARD, REVERSE_A, target, max_mismatches=0)
        print_report(f"Case 15: primer Y, genome {genome_base}", result)
        check(site_of(result, "forward")["mismatches"] == 0, f"Y matches genome {genome_base}")

    target = filler(10) + mutate(amplicon(), 9, "A") + filler(10)
    result = run_model(DEGENERATE_FORWARD, REVERSE_A, target, max_mismatches=1)
    print_report("Case 15: primer Y, genome A", result)
    check(site_of(result, "forward")["changes"] ==
          [{"from_3prime": 11, "primer": "Y", "genome": "A", "severity": "mild"}],
          "Y does not match genome A: 11 from 3' end, primer Y, genome A, mild")


# -- Case 16: probe binds inside the product ---------------------------------
# Probe = the 26-base insert, which sits between the primer sites.
def case_probe_binds():
    target = filler(10) + amplicon() + filler(10)
    result = run_model(FORWARD_A, REVERSE_A, target, probe=PROBE_A, max_mismatches=0)
    print_report("Case 16: probe binds inside the product", result)
    check(result["products"][0]["probe"] == "binds", "probe binds inside the 70 bp product")
    check(result["assay"] == "product", "assay is 'product'")


# -- Case 17: primers bind but the probe does not ----------------------------
# Three real mismatches in the insert (amplicon offsets 24, 32, 40), tolerance 1.
# Both primers still bind and copy the DNA, but the probe cannot bind, so a
# qPCR machine would see no fluorescence: "no signal".
def case_probe_mismatched():
    seq = amplicon()
    for offset in (24, 32, 40):
        seq = change_base(seq, offset)
    target = filler(10) + seq + filler(10)
    result = run_model(FORWARD_A, REVERSE_A, target, probe=PROBE_A, max_mismatches=1)
    print_report("Case 17: probe has 3 mismatches", result)
    check(result["outcomes"]["forward"] == "binds" and result["outcomes"]["reverse"] == "binds",
          "both primers bind")
    check(result["products"][0]["probe"] == "mismatched", "the probe does not bind")
    check(result["assay"] == "no signal", "assay is 'no signal'")


# -- Case 18: deletion inside a primer site ----------------------------------
# Delete 2 bases ("TA", amplicon offsets 6-7) from the 20-base forward site.
# Without gaps this looks like many mismatches; the near-miss search should
# explain it as ONE event: a 2-base deletion of primer bases 14 and 13 from
# the 3' end. (Gaps longer than 1 base are never allowed to bind.)
def case_deletion():
    seq = amplicon()
    target = filler(10) + seq[:6] + seq[8:] + filler(10)
    result = run_model(FORWARD_A, REVERSE_A, target, max_mismatches=1)
    print_report("Case 18: 2-base deletion in the forward site", result)
    miss = result["near_misses"]["forward"]
    check(result["outcomes"]["forward"] == "mismatched", "forward is 'mismatched'")
    check(miss["events"] == 1, "near-miss is 1 event, not many mismatches")
    check(miss["indel"] == {"kind": "deletion", "length": 2, "from_3prime": (13, 14)},
          "explained as a 2-base deletion, 13-14 from the 3' end")


# -- Case 18b: a 6-base deletion is too long for an 18-base primer ----------
# Set B. Delete 6 bases (offsets 6-11) from the 18-base forward site: only
# 18 - 6 = 12 primer bases would still match, fewer than MIN_MATCHED_BASES
# (14), so the model refuses to guess.
def case_deletion_too_long():
    seq = amplicon_b()
    target = filler(10) + seq[:6] + seq[12:] + filler(10)
    result = run_model(FORWARD_B, REVERSE_B, target, max_mismatches=1)
    print_report("Case 18b: 6-base deletion in an 18-base primer site", result)
    check(result["outcomes"]["forward"] == "mismatched", "forward is 'mismatched'")
    check(result["near_misses"]["forward"] is None, "no near-miss: too few matching bases to be sure")


# -- Case 18c: the same 6-base deletion IS found in a 30-base primer --------
# Set B. Delete 6 bases from the middle of the 30-base reverse site (amplicon
# offsets 55-60 = site offsets 12-17): 30 - 6 = 24 bases still match (>= 14),
# so it is explained as ONE 6-base deletion, like Alpha's spike 69-70 deletion.
def case_deletion_long_primer():
    seq = amplicon_b()
    target = filler(10) + seq[:55] + seq[61:] + filler(10)
    result = run_model(FORWARD_B, REVERSE_B, target, max_mismatches=1)
    print_report("Case 18c: 6-base deletion in a 30-base primer site", result)
    miss = result["near_misses"]["reverse"]
    check(result["outcomes"]["reverse"] == "mismatched", "reverse is 'mismatched'")
    check(miss["events"] == 1, "near-miss is 1 event")
    check((miss["indel"]["kind"], miss["indel"]["length"]) == ("deletion", 6), "explained as a 6-base deletion")


# -- Case 19: insertion inside a primer site ---------------------------------
# Insert TTT into the middle of the 24-base reverse site (after amplicon offset 57).
def case_insertion():
    seq = amplicon()
    target = filler(10) + seq[:58] + "TTT" + seq[58:] + filler(10)
    result = run_model(FORWARD_A, REVERSE_A, target, max_mismatches=1)
    print_report("Case 19: 3-base insertion in the reverse site", result)
    miss = result["near_misses"]["reverse"]
    check(result["outcomes"]["reverse"] == "mismatched", "reverse is 'mismatched'")
    check(miss["events"] == 1, "near-miss is 1 event")
    check((miss["indel"]["kind"], miss["indel"]["length"]) == ("insertion", 3), "explained as a 3-base insertion")


# =============================================================================
# SECTION 5: CASES SOLVABLE BY HAND: VERSION 4 LOGIC FIXES
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Genome ambiguity codes, graded 3' risk, and binding through a small
# insertion/deletion in the primer's 5' half. (Case 7b above covers the
# "missing data cannot change the answer" fix.)
# =============================================================================

# -- Case 20: ambiguity codes in the genome ----------------------------------
# The forward primer has C at offset 9 (11 bases from the 3' end).
#   genome Y (C or T): might match, might not      -> unknown
#   genome R (A or G): cannot match a C             -> certain mismatch
#                      (template Y = C or T; C-C is severe -> severe)
#   primer Y vs genome Y: every option is accepted  -> certain match
def case_genome_ambiguity():
    target = filler(10) + mutate(amplicon(), 9, "Y") + filler(10)
    result = run_model(FORWARD_A, REVERSE_A, target, max_mismatches=0)
    print_report("Case 20a: primer C, genome Y", result)
    check(site_of(result, "forward")["unknown_from_3prime"] == [11], "genome Y is unknown, not a mismatch")
    check(result["outcomes"]["forward"] == "not assessable", "forward is 'not assessable'")

    target = filler(10) + mutate(amplicon(), 9, "R") + filler(10)
    result = run_model(FORWARD_A, REVERSE_A, target, max_mismatches=0)
    print_report("Case 20b: primer C, genome R, tolerance 0", result)
    check(result["outcomes"]["forward"] == "mismatched", "genome R is a certain mismatch: 'mismatched'")
    result = run_model(FORWARD_A, REVERSE_A, target, max_mismatches=1)
    print_report("Case 20b: primer C, genome R, tolerance 1", result)
    check(site_of(result, "forward")["changes"] ==
          [{"from_3prime": 11, "primer": "C", "genome": "R", "severity": "severe"}],
          "reported as primer C, genome R, severe")

    target = filler(10) + mutate(amplicon(), 9, "Y") + filler(10)
    result = run_model(DEGENERATE_FORWARD, REVERSE_A, target, max_mismatches=0)
    print_report("Case 20c: primer Y, genome Y", result)
    forward_site = site_of(result, "forward")
    check(forward_site["outcome"] == "binds" and forward_site["unknown_from_3prime"] == [],
          "primer Y fully accepts genome Y: a certain match")


# -- Case 21: graded 3' risk -------------------------------------------------
# a) Only the reverse site's 3'-terminal mismatch (amplicon offset 46 T -> C):
#    A-C is mild, so the product's 3' risk is LOW.
# b) The forward site's 3'-terminal base is N, tolerance 1: the site binds
#    even if the N is a mismatch, but the 3' end is uncertain: POSSIBLE.
def case_graded_risk():
    target = filler(10) + mutate(amplicon(), 46, "C") + filler(10)
    result = run_model(FORWARD_A, REVERSE_A, target, max_mismatches=1)
    print_report("Case 21a: one mild mismatch at the 3' end", result)
    check(result["products"][0]["three_prime_risk"] == "low", "product 3' risk is LOW")

    target = filler(10) + mutate(amplicon(), 19, "N") + filler(10)
    result = run_model(FORWARD_A, REVERSE_A, target, max_mismatches=1)
    print_report("Case 21b: N at the forward primer's 3' end", result)
    check(site_of(result, "forward")["outcome"] == "binds", "forward binds even if the N is a mismatch")
    check(result["products"][0]["three_prime_risk"] == "possible", "product 3' risk is POSSIBLE")


# -- Case 22: 1-base deletion in the primer's 5' half ------------------------
# Delete amplicon offset 2 (a G, 18 bases from the 3' end; the G beside it
# makes 17 an equally good answer). Both are more than 20 // 2 = 10 from the
# 3' end, so the 3' half is intact and with 1 mismatch allowed the forward
# primer still binds, counting the gap as 1 mismatch.
# The product loses 1 base: 69 bp. With 0 mismatches allowed it does not bind.
def case_small_deletion_5prime():
    seq = amplicon()
    target = filler(10) + seq[:2] + seq[3:] + filler(10)
    result = run_model(FORWARD_A, REVERSE_A, target, max_mismatches=1)
    print_report("Case 22: 1-base deletion in the 5' half, tolerance 1", result)
    forward_site = site_of(result, "forward")
    check((forward_site["indel"]["kind"], forward_site["indel"]["length"]) == ("deletion", 1),
          "forward binds through a 1-base deletion")
    check(forward_site["indel"]["from_3prime"][0] in (17, 18), "the deletion is 17 or 18 from the 3' end (5' half)")
    check(product_lengths(result) == [69], "product is 69 bp (one base shorter)")

    result = run_model(FORWARD_A, REVERSE_A, target, max_mismatches=0)
    print_report("Case 22: same, tolerance 0", result)
    check(result["outcomes"]["forward"] == "mismatched", "with 0 allowed the gap is too much")


# -- Case 22b: 1-base deletion in the primer's 3' half -----------------------
# Delete amplicon offset 16 (a G, 4 bases from the 3' end; its neighbours T and
# A differ, so the spot is unambiguous). Read without a gap, the site's last
# 4 bases GTCC face TCCC: 2 mismatches, more than the allowance of 1. A gap
# that close to the 3' end is not allowed to bind; the near-miss search
# explains it as a 1-base deletion 4 from the 3' end.
def case_small_deletion_3prime():
    seq = amplicon()
    target = filler(10) + seq[:16] + seq[17:] + filler(10)
    result = run_model(FORWARD_A, REVERSE_A, target, max_mismatches=1)
    print_report("Case 22b: 1-base deletion in the 3' half", result)
    check(result["outcomes"]["forward"] == "mismatched", "forward is 'mismatched'")
    check(result["near_misses"]["forward"]["indel"] ==
          {"kind": "deletion", "length": 1, "from_3prime": (4, 4)},
          "near-miss: 1-base deletion 4 bases from the 3' end")


# =============================================================================
# SECTION 6: CHECKING THE SEARCH ITSELF
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The k-mer search is fast because it skips most positions. These checks make
# sure it never skips a real site, and never invents near-misses.
# =============================================================================

def brute_force_sites(primer, target, max_mismatches):
    """The slow way: compare the primer at EVERY position on both strands."""
    found = set()
    for strand, pattern in (("+", primer), ("-", reverse_complement(primer))):
        for start in range(-len(pattern) + 1, len(target)):
            mismatches, unknowns = compare_site(target, start, pattern)
            if len(mismatches) <= max_mismatches and len(pattern) - len(unknowns) >= MIN_KNOWN_BASES:
                found.add((strand, start))
    return found


def random_test_target(rng, primer):
    """A 300-base random target with mutated primer copies, Ns/Ys and maybe a cut end."""
    target = [rng.choice("ACGT") for _ in range(300)]
    for _ in range(4):
        copy = list(primer if rng.random() < 0.5 else reverse_complement(primer))
        for _ in range(rng.randint(0, 3)):
            copy[rng.randrange(len(copy))] = rng.choice("ACGT")
        position = rng.randrange(-6, 300 - len(copy) + 6)
        for i, base in enumerate(copy):
            if 0 <= position + i < len(target):
                target[position + i] = base
    for i in range(len(target)):
        if rng.random() < 0.02:
            target[i] = rng.choice("NY")
    return "".join(target)


# -- Case 23: fast search finds exactly what the slow search finds -----------
# Primers of 18, 20, 24 and 30 bases x 50 random targets each x mismatch
# allowances 0, 1 and 2. Plain (ungapped) sites from the model must equal the
# slow every-position search exactly.
def case_search_complete():
    print("\n--- Case 23: fast search vs slow every-position search ---")
    rng = random.Random(23)
    searches, compared = 0, 0
    for primer in (FORWARD_B, FORWARD_A, REVERSE_A, REVERSE_B):
        for _ in range(50):
            target = random_test_target(rng, primer)
            for max_mismatches in (0, 1, 2):
                result = run_model(primer, FORWARD_A, target, max_mismatches=max_mismatches)
                fast = {(s["strand"], s["start"]) for s in result["sites"]
                        if s["primer"] == "forward" and s["indel"] is None}
                slow = brute_force_sites(primer, target, max_mismatches)
                if fast != slow:
                    raise AssertionError(f"{primer}: fast {sorted(fast)} != slow {sorted(slow)} for {target}")
                searches += 1
                compared += len(slow)
    check(True, f"{searches} searches agree with the slow search ({compared} sites compared)")


# -- Case 24: no invented near-misses on a random genome ---------------------
# A random 30,000-base sequence (the size of SARS-CoV-2) should not contain
# the CDC N1 primers or probe, and the near-miss search must not invent a
# "close" site there. (Before the MIN_MATCHED_BASES rule, it did.)
def case_random_genome():
    print("\n--- Case 24: CDC N1 primers on a random 30,000-base sequence ---")
    rng = random.Random(24)
    genome = "".join(rng.choice("ACGT") for _ in range(30000))
    result = run_model("GACCCCAAAATCAGCGAAAT", "TCTGGTTACTGCCAGTTGAATCTG", genome,
                       probe="ACCCCGCATTACGTTTGGTGGACC")
    check(result["sites"] == [], "no binding sites")
    check(all(miss is None for miss in result["near_misses"].values()), "no near-misses invented")

    case_search_complete()
    case_random_genome()
    print("\nAll cases passed.")

from test_first_model_factor_specificity import *

F = filler
A, B = amplicon(), amplicon_b()
P = "  Target:   "

def T(seq, marks=(), note=None):
    out = P + seq
    if marks:
        line = [" "] * len(seq)
        for m in marks:
            line[m] = "^"
        out += "\n" + " " * len(P) + "".join(line).rstrip()
        if note:
            out += "   " + note

def muts(seq, offsets):

old = open("/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-isabelguo-programming-project/af9073fb-1deb-430d-a6d0-1f88d8b92ec4/scratchpad/cases_old.txt").read()

text = f"""TEST CASES: FIRST MODEL: FACTOR: SPECIFICITY (version 4)
=========================================================
Model: journal/first_model_factor_specificity.py
Tests: journal/test_first_model_factor_specificity.py
Run:   python3 journal/test_first_model_factor_specificity.py
Real-data check: python3 journal/cdc_reference_check.py  (see the end of this file)

All cases use fake primers and probes of 18-30 bases (the range of real
qPCR oligos; the CDC ones are 18-24) and a fake target built by hand, so
every expected answer is worked out on paper before running.

Fake pieces, set A (used by most cases):
  Forward primer   {FORWARD_A}              (20 bases)
  Reverse primer   {REVERSE_A}          (24 bases)
  Reverse site     {REVERSE_SITE_A}          (reverse primer as it appears on the + strand)
  Insert / probe   {INSERT_A}        (26 bases)
  Amplicon         forward + insert + reverse site = 20 + 26 + 24 = 70 bp
                   (amplicon offsets: forward 0-19, insert 20-45, reverse 46-69)

Fake pieces, set B (cases about primer length):
  Forward primer   {FORWARD_B}                (18 bases)
  Reverse primer   {REVERSE_B}    (30 bases)
  Reverse site     {REVERSE_SITE_B}
  Insert           {INSERT_B}         (25 bases)
  Amplicon         18 + 25 + 30 = 73 bp
                   (amplicon offsets: forward 0-17, insert 18-42, reverse 43-72)

  Filler           AAAA...            (poly-A; no primer contains AAAAA or
                                       TTTTT, so none can bind it)

Outcomes:
  Primer/probe: binds / mismatched / not assessable
  Assay:        product / not assessable / no signal / no product
  Positions are 1-based (first base of the target = 1).
  ^ marks a planted mismatch, N or extra base in the target.
  Base changes read "primer C, genome G": the primer has C where a
  perfect primer would need G (both in the primer's own direction).
  Severity: severe (primer-template A-A, G-A, A-G, C-C) or mild (all others).
  3' risk: high (severe mismatch within 3 bases of the 3' end), low (mild
  only), possible (unknown base there), or none.


CORE CASES (version 1)
----------------------

Case 1a - Exact match
  Mismatches allowed: 0
{T(F(10)+A+F(10))}
  Outcome:  forward binds (11-30), reverse binds (57-80)
            -> product, 70 bp (positions 11-80)
  Meaning:  Baseline: perfect primers give exactly one product of the right
            size. If this fails, nothing else can be trusted.

Case 1b - Exact match, set B (18- and 30-base primers)
  Mismatches allowed: 0
{T(F(10)+B+F(10))}
  Outcome:  forward binds (11-28), reverse binds (54-83)
            -> product, 73 bp (positions 11-83)
  Meaning:  The model is not tied to one primer length: the shortest and
            longest lengths in the 18-30 range work too.

Case 2 - Reverse strand
  Mismatches allowed: 0
{T(reverse_complement(F(10)+A+F(10)))}
            (Case 1a target, reverse-complemented)
  Outcome:  forward binds, reverse binds -> product, 70 bp
            (the reverse primer is now the "+" site, forward the "-" site)
  Meaning:  Primers can bind either DNA strand; a model checking only one
            strand would miss real products.

Case 3a - Mismatches at the 3' end, none allowed
  Mismatches allowed: 0
{T(F(10)+mutate(mutate(A,19,"G"),46,"C")+F(10), [29,56])}
  Outcome:  forward mismatched, reverse mismatched -> no product
            near-misses: forward 1 from 3': primer C, genome G (severe)
                         reverse 1 from 3': primer A, genome G (mild)
  Meaning:  With zero tolerance, one mismatch per primer loses the product,
            and the near-miss says exactly which base change caused it.

Case 3b - Same target, 1 mismatch allowed
  Mismatches allowed: 1
  Target:   (same as 3a)
  Outcome:  forward binds, reverse binds -> product, 70 bp
            forward site 3' risk HIGH (C opposite template C: severe)
            reverse site 3' risk LOW  (A opposite template C: mild)
            product takes the worse grade: HIGH; WARNING printed
  Meaning:  The user-set allowance works, and 3'-end mismatches are graded
            by how much that kind of mismatch actually hurts PCR.

Case 3c - Mismatch at the 5' end
  Mismatches allowed: 1
{T(F(10)+mutate(A,0,"G")+F(10), [10])}
  Outcome:  forward binds (20 from 3': primer A, genome G, mild), reverse
            binds -> product, 70 bp, no 3' risk
  Meaning:  Position counting runs the right direction, and a harmless 5'
            mismatch does not raise a warning.

Case 4 - Multiple products
  Mismatches allowed: 0
{T(F(10)+A+F(30)+A+F(10))}
            (two copies of the amplicon, at 11-80 and 111-180)
  Outcome:  forward binds, reverse binds -> 3 products: 70, 70 and 170 bp
  Meaning:  Primers that bind more than one place make extra products,
            including a long one spanning both copies.

Case 4b - Same target, max product length 100
  Mismatches allowed: 0
  Target:   (same as 4)
  Outcome:  forward binds, reverse binds -> 2 products: 70 and 70 bp
  Meaning:  The product length limit removes implausibly long products.

Case 5 - Primers facing away
  Mismatches allowed: 0
{T(F(10)+REVERSE_SITE_A+INSERT_A+FORWARD_A+F(10))}
            (reverse site first, forward site second)
  Outcome:  forward binds, reverse binds -> no product
  Meaning:  Binding alone is not enough; the primers must face each other.

Case 6 - No site
  Mismatches allowed: 2
  Target:   200 x A
  Outcome:  forward mismatched, reverse mismatched -> no product
            no near-miss ("none close")
  Meaning:  Guards against false positives.


BAD-DATA CASES (version 2)
--------------------------

Case 7 - Ns inside a primer site
  Mismatches allowed: 0
{T(F(10)+mutate(mutate(A,5,"N"),6,"N")+F(10), [15,16])}
  Outcome:  forward not assessable (0 mismatches, Ns 14 and 15 bases from
            the 3' end), reverse binds -> not assessable
  Meaning:  Poorly sequenced regions are written as N. They are missing data,
            not mutations, so they are not counted as mismatches.

Case 7b - Same Ns, 2 mismatches allowed (version 4)
  Mismatches allowed: 2
  Target:   (same as 7)
  Outcome:  forward binds ("binds even if every unknown base is a mismatch"),
            reverse binds -> product, 70 bp
  Meaning:  0 mismatches + 2 unknown = 2, which still fits the allowance.

Mostly right, with a few corrections. The biggest one is that **k is still 5**. We talked about k = 6 but never changed it; `run_model` still has `k=5`.

**Corrections**

1. **IUPAC checking applies to the primers and probe, not to every base.** `clean_oligo` rejects any primer letter that isn't a DNA or IUPAC code. The genome isn't rejected. Its ambiguity codes are read as match, mismatch or unknown, and anything else (like `-`) counts as unknown.
2. **Reverse complement:** the code doesn't build a second genome strand. To find where a primer binds the − strand, it searches the + strand for the primer's reverse complement. Both the forward and reverse primers are searched on both strands.
3. **Only the genome is indexed.** The k-mer index (k = 5) is built from the target genome. Primers are split into pieces, and the first 5 bases of each piece are looked up as seeds (the pigeonhole guarantee). Every hit is then checked against the full primer.
4. **Two separate grades, not one:**
   - Each mismatch gets a **severity**: severe (A-A, G-A, A-G, C-C) or mild (everything else).
   - Each site gets a **3′ risk** from mismatches within 3 bases of the 3′ end: high (a severe one there), low (only mild ones there), possible (an unknown base there), or none.
5. **There are three outcomes, not two:** binds, **mismatched**, and not assessable.

**Steps your summary left out**

6. **Gaps in the 5′ half:** a 1-base insertion or deletion in the primer's 5′ half still binds, and counts as 1 mismatch.
7. **Near-miss search:** for a primer that fails, the code finds the closest site and explains it, including one insertion or deletion of up to 6 bases.
8. **Products:** a + site facing a downstream − site, 20–1000 bp apart, makes a product. Primers can also pair with themselves.
9. **Probe check:** the probe must bind inside the product. If it doesn't, the result is "no signal".
10. **Assay outcome:** product, not assessable, no signal, or no product.

So one sentence version: check the primer letters → search the genome's 5-mer index with seeds from the primer and its reverse complement → compare each candidate to the full primer → grade mismatches and 3′ risk → assign binds / mismatched / not assessable → pair sites into products → check the probe → give the assay outcome.

There's also a FASTA reader, the hand-solvable tests you just had redone, and the CDC check on the reference genome.

k is now 6, and the hand-solvable tests reflect it. All tests pass, and the suite takes 10.5 s instead of 18.5 s. The CDC reference check and the variant check give exactly the same results as with k = 5.

**The k = 6 change** (`first_model_factor_specificity.py`)
- `run_model` now defaults to `k=6`.
- Section 2 has a new note on why: a random 6-mer appears about 7 times in a 30 kb genome, against about 29 for a 5-mer. The cost is that primers must be at least 6 × (mismatches + 1) long, which is 18 nt at the default of 2 mismatches.
- The limit comments now say 6. Near-misses are guaranteed to be found with up to 2 events for 18- and 20-nt primers, up to 3 for 24 nt, and up to 4 for 30 nt.

# Modification Documentation: First Model, Factor: Specificity

Every problem found in the specificity model and how it was fixed, in the
order it happened, with the technical details.

**Reading alongside `diary.md`:** both files use the same logs in the same
order. The diary says what was done in plain words; this file gives the
problem, the fix, and the functions and settings involved. Items are
numbered, and the diary points to them as **(#n)**.

**Files** (all in `journal/`):

| File | Contents |
|---|---|
| `first_model_factor_specificity.py` | the model |
| `test_first_model_factor_specificity.py` | hand-solvable tests + search checks |
| `cdc_reference_check.py` | CDC panel on the real reference genome |
| `test_cases_specificity.txt` | every test case and its outcome |
| `diary.md` | plain-language log of each version |

---

## Log 6 · 2026-10-30 · First variant results (quick first pass)

**Commits:** `f0b44dd`, `761fe07` (#35), `5834b32` (#36), then #37 and the session logs (filled in at the next update)

**#33. Problem:** the model had only been run on the reference genome, not on
the variants the project asks about.
**Fix:** new `variant_check.py` reuses `read_assays`, `PRIMER_TABLE`,
`REFERENCE` and `MAX_MISMATCHES` from `cdc_reference_check.py` and calls
`run_model` (allowance 2, probe included) for N1/N2/N3 on the reference and
every `data/variants/*.fasta`. For each oligo, `fewest_mismatches` reports
the lowest mismatch count among its binding sites; the table also shows the
assay outcome, product size and 3' risk. Result: every assay gives a product
on Alpha, Delta and Omicron (N1 72, N2 67, N3 72 bp, as on the reference);
the only mismatch is 1 in the N1 probe on Omicron; no 3' risk.
Limit: one isolate per variant.

**#34. Problem:** the genome files had mangled names
(`data:reference:NC_045512.2.fasta.`, `OmicronBA.1_OL672836.1.`) and the
variants had no `.fasta` extension.
**Fix:** renamed with `git mv` to `NC_045512.2.fasta`,
`Alpha_B.1.1.7_MZ068155.fasta`, `Delta_B.1.617.2_MZ555945.fasta` and
`Omicron_BA.1_OL672836.1.fasta`. `cdc_reference_check.py` finds the reference
with a glob, so it needed no change (same results).

**#35. Problem:** `.DS_Store` files (3 committed) kept showing as modified,
even though `.gitignore` lists `.DS_Store` (it only stops new files), and
`journal/__pycache__/` appeared after running the scripts.
**Fix:** added `__pycache__/` to `.gitignore`; the committed `.DS_Store` files were removed from the repo with
`git rm --cached` (kept on disk).

**#36. Problem:** the N1 size question from #23 (72 bp computed vs 73 bp in
the table) was still open, so `cdc_reference_check.py` reported 1 FAIL.
**Fix:** the table's own coordinates (published 28303–28374, verified
28287–28358) both give 72 bases, the reference genome gives 72, and the JRC
SARS-CoV-2 diagnostics database lists the CDC N1 product as 72 bp. The 73 was
a data-entry error: `pub_amplicon_bp` for N1 in
`data/primers/CDC primer sequences.tsv` changed from 73 to 72. All CDC
reference checks now pass.

**#37. Problem:** #33 found 1 mismatch in the N1 probe on Omicron but did
not say where it is or whether it is a real lineage mutation.
**Finding:** a one-off comparison of the reference and
`Omicron_BA.1_OL672836.1.fasta` at the N1 probe site (28309–28332) puts it at
**28311, C→T**, base 3 from the probe's 5' end. This is the known Omicron
mutation **N:P13L** (nucleocapsid codon 13, proline → leucine), so it is a
lineage change, not an isolate quirk. No code changed.
Note (from reading `find_binding_sites` and `product_status`): mismatch
severity and `three_prime_risk` are labels only. The binds/product decision
uses the mismatch count alone, so a severe 3' mismatch still gives
"product" with a `[3' RISK: HIGH]` warning.

---

## Still open (known limits after version 4)
- Near-miss and small-gap searches need an exact 5-base stretch (#15).
- Near-miss limits (#16, #17) were tuned on random sequence, not real genomes
  with repeats.
- Severity is a two-level rule (#20); real effects also depend on
  neighbouring bases and positions beyond the 3' window.
- Sites running off the start print negative positions (e.g. -3-48).
- Input is not cleaned of pasted spaces or line breaks.
- The k-mer index is rebuilt on every run; the test suite takes ~14 s.
- The mismatch allowance can only be changed in the code.
- Variants checked with one isolate each (#33).
- Severity and 3' risk do not change the outcome; only the mismatch count
  decides "binds" (#37).
- Binding is yes/no: a mismatch that still binds (e.g. the Omicron N1 probe,
  #37) may lower efficiency or probe signal and give a later Ct, which the
  model cannot show yet.

## Planned (not built yet)
- **Factor 2: melting temperature (Tm), nearest-neighbor model.** Sum the
  SantaLucia (1998) stack values in `data/thermodynamics/santalucia_1998_nn.tsv`
  (ΔH, ΔS, plus initiation and symmetry terms) and use
  Tm = ΔH / (ΔS + R·ln(C/4)) − 273.15.
  - **Salt correction:** the table is for 1 M NaCl, but
    `primer3_reference_tm.tsv` used 50 mM monovalent, 3 mM Mg²⁺, 0.8 mM dNTP,
    250 nM oligo. Add a monovalent + Mg²⁺ correction (dNTPs bind some Mg²⁺);
    find out which correction Primer3 uses, then match its Tm values as the
    first check.
  - **Mismatch parameters:** the table has only the 10 matched stacks. Add the
    Allawi & SantaLucia (1997–1998) mismatch stack values so Tm can be
    computed on a variant's real site (G·T is mild, C·C or A·A much worse).
  - **Compare with the annealing temperature** of the CDC protocol (about
    55 °C; to be checked against the protocol) and report each oligo's Tm
    drop per variant. First target: the N1 probe on Omicron (C28311T, #37).
- **Fraction bound at the annealing temperature.** Tm is only the 50% point;
  ΔG at the annealing temperature gives the fraction of oligo bound, a step
  from yes/no binding toward lost efficiency and a predicted Ct shift.
- **Probe-specific check (TaqMan).** The probe is cleaved by the polymerase
  only if bound when it arrives; CDC probes sit about 10 °C above the primers
  (N1 probe 71.2 °C vs 60.6 / 64.5 °C). A probe mismatch can leave
  amplification intact but lower the signal, so the Ct comes later and the
  amount looks lower (a possible false negative near the cycle-40 cutoff).
  Report probe Tm margin separately from primer Tm.
- **Let 3' risk affect the outcome** (optional): e.g. a HIGH 3' risk marks the
  product "at risk" instead of a plain "product" (#37).
- **Later factors:** hairpins and primer-dimers (Primer3 ΔG columns already in
  `primer3_reference_tm.tsv`), the RT step (reverse primer starts the cDNA;
  RNA secondary structure at the site), and the CDC run conditions (primer and
  probe concentrations, cycling).
- **More genomes per variant**, and confirm C28311T across Omicron BA.1
  sequences (#33, #37).
- **Spike-targeting comparison assay.** Hypothesis: oligos in regions under
  strong selection (spike, especially the receptor-binding domain and
  antibody sites) gain mismatches across variants faster than oligos in
  functionally constrained regions (CDC N1/N2/N3 in the N gene). The change
  is driven by selection, not GC content, and shows up over months as
  variants replace one another, not within a few replication cycles.
  Plan: add a spike primer/probe set (e.g. a TaqPath-style S target) to
  `data/primers/`, run it with `run_model` alongside N1/N2/N3 in
  `variant_check.py`, and compare mismatch counts and `three_prime_risk` per
  variant. A primer across Alpha's ΔH69/V70 (about 21765–21770) doubles as
  the positive control (should fail on Alpha and Omicron BA.1, which also
  carries the deletion).

# Project Diary: Do early SARS-CoV-2 qPCR primers still match later variants?

02-120 Programming for Scientists · Isabel Guo

One log per version of the model, see also `modification documentation.md`.
The numbers in brackets, like **(#2)**, point to its matching numbered items.

---

## Log 1 · 2026-10-29 · Version 1: First model, factor: specificity

**Commit:** `8e3f1c3`

### What the model does, in plain words

A PCR test works by two short pieces of DNA, called **primers**, sticking to
the virus's genome and copying the stretch between them. If the virus
mutates where a primer sticks, the primer may not stick anymore, and the test
can miss the virus.

This first model asks one simple question: **"Where would these two primers
stick, and would they copy anything?"**

1. **Make a lookup table of the genome.** Like the index at the back of a
   book, it records where every short 5-letter word appears, so the program
   doesn't have to read the whole genome for every primer.
2. **Find where each primer sticks.** It looks on both strands of the DNA
   (DNA is double-stranded, and a primer can stick to either one) and lets
   you choose how many wrong letters (mismatches) are still OK. That setting
   is marked with a star banner so it's easy to find **(#1)**.
3. **Say where the mistakes are.** Each mismatch is counted from the primer's
   **3' end**, the end where copying starts. A mistake there matters most.
4. **Pair the primers into products.** A copy (product) is only made when
   one primer points right, the other points left, and they face each other
   at a sensible distance.

It was tested on **made-up primers and a made-up DNA sequence**, so every
answer could be worked out by hand first (7 test cases).

**Not included yet:** melting temperature, primer dimers, real genomes.

### Core functions
| Function | What it does |
|---|---|
| `reverse_complement` | Gives the other DNA strand, so primers can be found on both strands |
| `build_kmer_index` | The lookup table: where every 5-letter word appears |
| `find_binding_sites` | Finds every spot a primer sticks within the mismatch allowance |
| `distances_from_3prime` | Counts each mismatch's distance from the 3' end |
| `pair_into_products` | Pairs facing sites into PCR products |
| `predict_products` | Runs the whole model in one call |

---


-----
## Log 6 · 2026-10-30 · First variant results (quick first pass)

**Commits:** `f0b44dd`, `761fe07` (#35), `5834b32` (#36), then #37 and the session logs (filled in at the next update)

### What I did
- Wrote a quick script, `variant_check.py`, that runs the CDC N1, N2 and N3
  assays on the reference and on the Alpha, Delta and Omicron genomes and
  prints one table **(#33)**.
- First answer: all three assays still give a product on all three variants,
  at the same sizes as on the reference. The only change is one mismatch in
  the N1 probe on Omicron, and no primer has a mismatch near its 3' end
  **(#33)**.
- Renamed the genome files to clean `.fasta` names, so the program can find
  them and the names say which variant each one is **(#34)**.
- Set git to ignore Mac `.DS_Store` files and Python's `__pycache__` folder,
  so they stop showing up as changes **(#35)**.
- Settled the N1 size question: the primer positions span 72 bases, the
  genome gives 72, and an outside database also says 72, so the 73 in my table
  was a typo. I changed it to 72 and every CDC check now passes **(#36)**.
- Found where the Omicron N1 probe mismatch is: genome position 28311, a C
  changed to T, the 3rd base of the probe. It is a known Omicron mutation
  (N:P13L), not just something odd about my one genome **(#37)**.
- Learned that my model only uses the number of mismatches to decide
  "binds". How bad a mismatch is and its 3' risk are only shown as warnings,
  so I need to read that column too **(#37)**.
- Went over the qPCR background: primers on opposite strands, cycles, Ct
  (the cycle where the signal crosses the threshold), ΔCt and ΔΔCt with a
  reference gene, fold change = 2^(−ΔΔCt), why the threshold sits in the
  exponential phase, melting temperature (Tm), and how a TaqMan probe makes
  the signal.

### Things to work on for next time
- Use more than one genome per variant, since one isolate may not be typical,
  and check that the C28311T change is in other Omicron BA.1 genomes too.
- Add the positive control from the proposal: a primer across Alpha's spike
  69-70 deletion must fail on the Alpha genome.
- Start the next factor: melting temperature (Tm) with the nearest-neighbor
  model, checked against the Primer3 values in `data/primers/`. Then work out
  each primer's Tm on each variant (mismatches lower it) and compare it with
  the test's annealing temperature (about 55 °C in the CDC protocol; check
  this). A Tm that drops close to it means the primer binds poorly.
  - The SantaLucia table I have is for 1 M salt, but the Primer3 values used
    50 mM salt and 3 mM magnesium, so I need a salt correction before the
    numbers can match.
  - I also need the mismatch values (Allawi & SantaLucia), since my table
    only has perfectly matched pairs.
  - Start with the N1 probe on Omicron: how much does C28311T lower its Tm?
- Look at the probe separately. A TaqMan probe only gives light if it is
  bound when the polymerase reaches it, so a weaker probe can make the Ct
  come later and the virus look like less than it is, even when the primers
  work fine.
- Go one step past Tm: work out how much of the primer is bound at the
  annealing temperature, as a step toward predicting a Ct shift.
- Maybe let a high 3' risk change the result instead of only showing a
  warning.
- Later: hairpins and primer-dimers, the RT step, and the CDC run conditions.
- Maybe add a spike-targeting primer set to compare with the CDC N assays. My
  idea: spike changes faster because the virus gains from escaping immunity
  there, while the N gene regions the CDC picked are more constrained. So a
  spike primer should pick up more mismatches across Alpha, Delta and Omicron.
  This happens over months as new variants take over, not in a few rounds of
  copying. A primer across Alpha's spike 69-70 deletion would also be the
  positive control above.

---

## Where things stand
Still open after version 4 (details at the end of
`modification documentation.md`): a few search limits, and binding is
still yes/no. The first variant run (Log 6) used only one genome per variant.
Next: melting temperature (factor 2); the plan is under "Planned" at the end
of `modification documentation.md`.

message.content: what does anchors do

content.text:
Anchors are the near-miss search's way of guessing where a failed primer might almost bind. They're used by `anchors_for` at `first_model_factor_specificity.py:480`, which feeds the near-miss search (`find_near_miss`) and the small-gap binding search (`find_indel_sites`).

**What it does:** it slides along the primer (or its reverse complement) and takes every 6-base stretch (k-mer), not just one per piece. It looks each one up in the genome index. For each hit, it works out where the primer would have to start for that stretch to line up:

```
anchor = genome position of the hit − where that stretch sits in the primer
```

**Example:** primer offset 7 is the start of the stretch `AGCATT`. If `AGCATT` is found at genome position 107, the anchor is 107 − 7 = 100. "If this primer binds near here, it starts at position 100."

All anchors go into a set, so if several stretches point to the same start, it's only checked once.

**What happens next:** each anchor is a starting point, not an answer. `placements` then tries the primer at that anchor:

- straight, with no gap
- with a deletion or insertion of 1–6 bases at every position along the primer, shifted both ways, because the matching stretch may sit on either side of the gap

Each placement is scored by events (mismatches + one indel), and the best one that meets the limits is kept.

**How this differs from the seeds in the main binding search:**

| | Main binding search (seeds) | Near-miss search (anchors) |
|---|---|---|
| Stretches looked up | first k bases of each piece | every k-base stretch in the primer |
| Why | the pigeonhole principle guarantees one clean piece | no guarantee, since an indel can shift everything, so it casts a wider net |
| Gaps tried | no | yes, up to 6 bases |

**The limit (#15, #40):** an anchor only exists if at least one 6-base stretch of the primer matches the genome exactly. If the differences break the primer into stretches all shorter than 6, there are no anchors, so the result is "none close". That's what Cases 10 and 10b show.

message.content: the gap, is a gap in the sequence? that differs form the primer

content.text:
Yes. A gap is where the genome and the primer don't line up base for base, because one has extra bases the other doesn't. It's drawn as a dash in an alignment. The code has two kinds, defined at `first_model_factor_specificity.py:411`:

**Deletion:** the genome is missing bases that the primer has.

```
primer:  ACGGTCTAGCATTGCAGTCC
genome:  ACGGTC--GCATTGCAGTCC      ← "TA" is gone from the genome
```

The 2 primer bases opposite the dashes have no genome partner (Case 18).

**Insertion:** the genome has extra bases that the primer doesn't.

```
primer:  TGACTGTCCAAG---CTGACTATCGGA
genome:  TGACTGTCCAAGTTTCTGACTATCGGA   ← "TTT" added in the genome
```

The 3 extra genome bases face nothing in the primer (Case 19).

**How this differs from a mismatch:** with a mismatch, the lengths still match and one base is just wrong (C where the primer wants G). With a gap, everything after it shifts by the gap length. Compared base by base without a gap, a single gap looks like many mismatches. Deleting "TA" above would make almost every later base look wrong. Trying gaps lets the code explain it as one event, which is the real mutation. That's how Alpha's 6-base spike deletion counts as 1 event, not 6 or more mismatches.

**In the code:**
- `gap_at`: where in the primer the gap sits
- `gap_length`: how many bases (1 to 6, `MAX_INDEL`)
- `kind`: `"deletion"` or `"insertion"`

**Two uses:**
- **Near-miss search:** gaps up to 6 bases, used only to explain why a primer failed.
- **Binding:** a 1-base gap in the primer's 5′ half still counts as "binds" and costs 1 mismatch (Case 22). A gap near the 3′ end never binds (Case 22b).

content.text:
Yes, that's right. A few details sharpen it.

**When it runs:** only for primers whose outcome is **mismatched**, meaning no site within the allowance. It's skipped for "binds" and for "not assessable", because missing data, not the primer, is the problem there.

**What it can report:**

| Result | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Mismatches only | a close site exists, but with more mismatches than allowed | Case 3a: 1 mismatch at the 3′ end, tolerance 0 |
| An indel (+ at most 1 mismatch) | the genome gained or lost bases at the site | Case 18: 2-base deletion; Case 19: 3-base insertion |
| "none close" | nothing close enough to report | Case 6: the primer's sequence isn't there at all |

**"none close" doesn't always mean there's no site.** It can mean any of these:

1. **There's really nothing similar** (Case 6).
2. **The site is too different to trust**, beyond these limits:
   - more than 4 mismatches, or more than 2 events when one is an indel
   - fewer than 14 primer bases matching (Case 18b: a 6-base deletion in an 18-nt primer)
   - an indel longer than 6 bases

   Matches that weak turn up by chance in a 30,000-base genome, so the code doesn't guess.
3. **The search couldn't see it.** No exact 6-base stretch is left to anchor on (Cases 10 and 10b), even though the site exists.

So the full order for each primer is:
1. Find binding sites within the mismatch allowance.
2. Try a 1-base gap in the 5′ half.
3. If both fail, run the near-miss search to explain why: too many mismatches, an indel, or none close.

content.text:
The file order is about helpers, not about the order things run. `describe_indel` is a small helper, and `find_indel_sites` is one of the functions that uses it.

**`describe_indel`** (line ~471) just labels a gap: it turns `kind`, `gap_at` and `gap_length` into something like `{"kind": "deletion", "length": 1, "from_3prime": (4, 4)}`. It doesn't search for anything.

**Two functions call it:**
- `find_near_miss` (Section 5) uses it to describe the gap in a failed primer's closest site.
- `find_indel_sites` (Section 5b) uses it to check whether a gap is in the 5′ half (`indel["from_3prime"][0] <= length // 2` means it isn't allowed).

Both also share `gapped_pairs`, `placements` and `anchors_for`. All the gap helpers sit in Section 5 with the near-miss search, and Section 5b comes after it so it can reuse them.

**File order vs. run order:**

| File order | Run order inside `run_model` |
|---|---|
| Section 4: `find_binding_sites` | 1. `find_binding_sites` |
| Section 5: gap helpers + `find_near_miss` | 2. `find_indel_sites` |
| Section 5b: `find_indel_sites` | 3. pairing, probe, outcomes |
| | 4. `find_near_miss` (failed primers only) |

Python doesn't need functions to appear in the file in the order they run. It only needs every function defined before `run_model` is actually called, and they all are by then.

Not quite. That check is about where the gap is, not how long it is. `find_indel_sites` uses two separate rules:

**1. Length:** at most 1 base (`MAX_BINDING_INDEL = 1`). This is enforced earlier, when the placements are generated:

```python
placements(anchor, length, MAX_BINDING_INDEL)   # only tries gaps of 1 base
```

Longer gaps are never even tried for binding. They only show up in the near-miss search, which goes up to 6.

**2. Position:** the gap must be in the primer's 5′ half. This is the line I quoted:

```python
if indel["from_3prime"][0] <= length // 2:
    continue  # gap is in the 3' half: not allowed to bind
```

`from_3prime[0]` is how far the gap's closest base is from the 3′ end. For a 20-nt primer, `length // 2` = 10:

| Gap position (from 3′) | Result |
|---|---|
| 18 (Case 22) | 18 > 10, so 5′ half: **binds**, costs 1 mismatch |
| 4 (Case 22b) | 4 ≤ 10, so 3′ half: **rejected**, then explained by the near-miss search |

**The biology behind it:** the polymerase starts copying at the 3′ end. A small gap near the 5′ end leaves the 3′ end paired, so copying can still start. A gap near the 3′ end disrupts the bases the polymerase needs, so the primer is treated as not binding.

So a 1-base gap near the 3′ end is rejected because of where it is, not its size. A 2-base gap anywhere is rejected because of its size.

content.text:
That's a fair challenge. The rule is a simplification, and the documentation (#21) never explains why the limit is 1. Here's the reasoning behind it, and where it falls short.

**Why a gap is treated as worse than the same number of mismatches**

1. **A mismatch keeps the alignment, a gap breaks it.** With 2 mismatches, the other 18 of 20 bases still pair normally, and the two bad pairs sit in an otherwise intact double helix. With a gap, the extra bases bulge out of the helix as a loop. Bulges bend and destabilize the duplex around them, and a 2-base bulge costs more than a 1-base one.
2. **The penalties are different sizes.** In nearest-neighbour thermodynamics, a 1-base bulge already costs about as much as a mismatch or more, and longer bulges cost more again. So a 2-base gap counted as "1 mismatch" would understate the damage.
3. **Chance matches.** A gap can sit at many positions, so allowing longer gaps gives random sequence many more ways to look like a binding site. That's the same problem the near-miss limits deal with (#16, #17).

**Where the rule is weak**
- The 1-base limit wasn't taken from measured data. It's a cautious cut-off.
- The rule isn't consistent. A 1-base gap counts as 1 mismatch, so with the default allowance of 2 you could have a 1-base gap plus 1 mismatch, but never a 2-base gap. Real binding depends on how much each change weakens the duplex, not on a count.
- Mismatches have the same problem. Two mismatches next to each other near the 3′ end are far worse than two spread out at the 5′ end, but both count as "2".

**The proper fix is the Tm factor you already planned.** The nearest-neighbour model scores mismatches and bulge loops on the same scale (ΔG), using published bulge-loop parameters. Then the question becomes "does this site still bind at the annealing temperature?", whatever mix of mismatches and gaps it has, with no separate 1-base rule.

For now I'd keep the rule and add a line to "Still open" saying the indel limit is a cut-off to be replaced by Tm-based scoring. I can add that note if you want.

content.text:
**Frameshifts don't matter for primer binding.** A frameshift is a protein idea: an insertion or deletion that isn't a multiple of 3 shifts how the gene is read in 3-base codons, so every amino acid after it is wrong. A primer never reads codons. It only pairs with DNA bases, so a 1-base and a 3-base indel affect binding in the same way, through the gap and bulge described above. Reading frame plays no part.

**Frameshifts still shape which indels you'll actually see.** In a viral gene, a frameshift usually wrecks the protein, so that virus dies out. The indels that survive in real variants are mostly multiples of 3: 3, 6 or 9 bases, which remove whole amino acids. That has two consequences for the model:

1. **The 1-base binding rule rarely matters in real variants.** Inside genes, 1-base indels are rare, so most real indels at a primer site will be 3 bases or more. The model always says those don't bind, and the near-miss search explains them.
2. **6-base indels are realistic.** Alpha's spike ΔH69/V70 is a 6-base deletion, which is why `MAX_INDEL = 6`.

**How a 6-base indel is handled now:**

| Primer length | Binds? | Near-miss |
|---|---|---|
| 18 nt | no | "none close": only 12 bases match, below the 14 needed (Case 18b) |
| 20–30 nt | no | found as 1 event, a 6-base deletion (Case 18c) |

"Doesn't bind" is reasonable here. A 6-base bulge in a 20-base duplex is very destabilizing, and if it's near the 3′ end, extension fails.

**One gap worth checking:** indels longer than 6 bases are never found. If I remember correctly, Omicron BA.1 also has a 9-base in-frame deletion in the N gene, N:ΔE31–S33, at about positions 28362–28370. That would sit just downstream of the N1 reverse primer site (28335–28358), which would explain why N1 still worked on Omicron in your variant check. Please check those coordinates against the genome; I'm going from memory.

If a 9-base deletion ever overlapped a primer site, the model would say "mismatched" with no explanation. The fix would be raising `MAX_INDEL` to 9. With 20–30 nt primers that still leaves at least 14 matched bases at a 9-base deletion for primers of 23 nt or more, but it gives random matches more chances, so Case 24 would need re-checking.

content.text:
No. The 14 has nothing to do with the mismatch allowance. They're separate settings for separate searches:

| Setting | Value | Used by | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `max_mismatches` | 2 (user setting) | binding search | how different a site can be and still **bind** |
| `MIN_MATCHED_BASES` | 14 (fixed) | near-miss search only | how much must match before a failed primer's near-miss is **reported** |

Changing `max_mismatches` to 0 or 3 leaves the 14 unchanged.

**Where the 14 came from (#16):** while building version 3, the CDC N1 primers were run on a random 30,000-base sequence, which shouldn't contain anything close. The near-miss search still reported a fake "6-base deletion + 1 mismatch". A long deletion leaves few bases to compare, and the search tries the gap at every position and in both directions, so a short stretch matching by chance becomes likely. Requiring at least 14 primer bases to match exactly stopped that.

The 14 was set empirically, by testing against random sequence, not derived from a formula. Case 24 re-checks it on every test run. Roughly, an exact 14-base match appears by chance about once in 4¹⁴ ≈ 270 million positions. That's far more than the 30,000 positions in a genome, but trying every gap position, both directions and a few mismatches multiplies the chances, so 14 leaves a safety margin rather than a huge one.

**What it means for indels:** the longest deletion that can be reported is primer length − 14:

| Primer | Longest reportable deletion |
|---|---|
| 18 nt | 4 bases |
| 20 nt | 6 bases |
| 23 nt | 9 bases, enough for a 9-base deletion like Omicron's N:ΔE31–S33, if `MAX_INDEL` were raised |
| 30 nt | 16 bases (but capped at `MAX_INDEL` = 6) |

So for the 9-base question, the 14 isn't the blocker for primers of 23 nt or longer. The cap of 6 in `MAX_INDEL` is.

content.text:
That wording was loose. It refers to what `placements` (line ~455) tries around each anchor. For every anchor it generates:

```python
for gap_length in 1..6:              # gap size
    for gap_at in 1..length-1:       # every position inside the primer
        insertion, with the primer start at anchor or anchor - gap_length
        deletion,  with the primer start at anchor or anchor + gap_length
```

**"Every position":** the gap is tried between every pair of neighbouring primer bases. For a 20-nt primer, that's positions 1–19:

```
gap_at = 1:   A|CGGTCTAGCATTGCAGTCC
gap_at = 2:   AC|GGTCTAGCATTGCAGTCC
...
gap_at = 19:  ACGGTCTAGCATTGCAGTC|C
```

**What I called "both directions"** means the matching seed could be on either side of the gap, not two DNA strands. The anchor comes from one exact 6-base stretch, but the code doesn't know whether that stretch is left or right of the gap:

```
seed LEFT of the gap:   [seed....]--[.......]   → primer starts at the anchor
seed RIGHT of the gap:  [.......]--[seed....]   → everything left of the gap shifts,
                                                   so the start moves by gap_length
```

That's why each gap is tried with two start positions. (The near-miss search does also run on both strands, + and −, as a separate loop.)

**Why this matters for chance matches:** for one anchor on a 20-nt primer, that's about

1 (no gap) + 6 sizes × 19 positions × 4 (insertion/deletion × 2 starts) ≈ **450 placements**

Every anchor, from every 6-base stretch on both strands, gets about 450 tries. That's many chances for random sequence to happen to fit, which is why the 14-matched-base rule and the event limits are needed. Each extra gap size you allow adds about 75 more tries per anchor, so raising `MAX_INDEL` to 9 would also raise the chance-match risk, and Case 24 would need re-checking.

content.text:
Not quite. The 14 doesn't decide binding, and it doesn't give a reason.

**Binding was already decided earlier,** by the mismatch allowance. A 20-nt primer with the default of 2 binds only if at least 18 bases match. Any site with fewer than 14 matching is far below that, so the primer has already failed before the 14 rule is ever checked.

**What the 14 decides:** whether the code can say why it failed.

| Bases matching at the closest site | Outcome | Explanation |
|---|---|---|
| enough for the allowance (e.g. ≥ 18 of 20) | binds | — |
| fewer, but ≥ 14, within the event limits | mismatched | near-miss reported: "these mismatches / this indel" |
| < 14 | mismatched | **"none close"**: no explanation |

**"none close" means "can't tell", not a proven incompatibility.** It could be either:
- there's no related site at all (the region is gone or the sequence is unrelated), or
- the real site is there but changed so much (for example, a big deletion) that it can't be told apart from a random match.

The code refuses to choose between those, rather than report a possibly fake explanation.

So the accurate version is: if fewer than 14 bases match, the primer doesn't bind (that was already decided by the allowance), and the model says it can't reliably explain why.

content.text:
A random match is a stretch of genome that happens to look like the primer by chance, not because it's the primer's real site that has mutated.

**Why they happen:** DNA has only 4 letters, so short patterns repeat constantly. In a 30,000-base genome:

| Pattern length | Possible sequences | Times you'd expect to see one by chance |
|---|---|---|
| 6 | 4,096 | ~7 |
| 10 | ~1 million | ~0.03 |
| 14 | ~270 million | ~0.0001 |
| 20 | ~1 trillion | essentially never |

(Counting both strands, about 60,000 positions.)

So a full 20-base exact match is meaningful: it's almost certainly the real site. A 6-base match means nothing on its own, since it appears about 7 times anyway.

**Why the near-miss search makes them more likely:** it doesn't ask for one exact pattern. It accepts a few mismatches, a gap of any size up to 6 at any position, and about 450 placements per anchor. Each extra freedom multiplies the number of ways random sequence can fit. Enough freedom and something will fit somewhere.

**The real example (#16):** the CDC N1 primer was run on a completely random 30,000-base sequence. There is no N1 site in it, mutated or otherwise. The near-miss search still reported "6-base deletion + 1 mismatch". That's a random match: with 6 bases deleted, only 13 of 20 primer bases were left to compare, and that's few enough that, given all those tries, a random stretch lined up.

**How the code guards against it:**
- At least **14 bases must match exactly** (`MIN_MATCHED_BASES`).
- At most **4 mismatches**, or **an indel + 1 mismatch** (the event limits).
- **Case 24** re-runs the random-sequence test on every run and checks that nothing is reported.
