**Two right, one half-right, one wrong.** I checked the code: the window is `from_3prime <= 3`, so 1, 2 and 3 bases from the 3′ end are all inside it.

| Variant | Your answer | Correct answer | |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | product, at risk | made, **product** (low 3′ risk warning) | ❌ |
| B | not made, mismatched | made, **at risk** | ❌ |
| C | product, low 3′ risk | made, **product**, 3′ risk **none** | ½ |
| D | made but can't see, no signal | made, **no signal** | ✅ |

**A.** A opposite C is **mild**: it isn't on the severe list. It's inside the window (1 ≤ 3), but mild there only gives **low**, so the status stays **"product"**. This is the same slip as Lab 2: being close to the 3′ end doesn't make a mismatch high risk unless the mismatch is also severe.

**B.** C opposite C **is severe**, and 3 from the 3′ end **is inside** the window (3 ≤ 3). That makes the risk **high**. But it's only **1 mismatch** (≤ 2), so the primer still **binds**, the product **is made**, and the status is **"at risk"**. "Mismatched" only happens when the count goes over the allowance or an indel isn't allowed.

**C.** The status "product" is right. A opposite G is severe, but 4 from the 3′ end is **outside** the window (4 > 3), so it doesn't affect 3′ risk at all. The risk is **none**, not low. It just counts as 1 mismatch toward the allowance.

**D ✅.** A 1-base indel counts as at most 1 mismatch (and only when it's in the 5′ half). With the 2 mismatches that's 3 > 2, so the probe is mismatched. The product is still made, but there's **no signal**.

Run these three checks in this order every time:

```
1. Count: mismatches (+ allowed indel) <= 2?          no → mismatched → no product
2. Window: any mismatch with from_3prime <= 3?        no → risk none   → "product"
3. Severity of the ones in the window: any severe?   yes → high       → "at risk"
                                                      no → low        → "product" (warning)
```

Your errors on A and C both came from skipping one of steps 2 and 3. A was close but not severe, and C was severe but not close. "At risk" needs both.

The commit is still pending whenever you're ready.

## Log 7 · 2026-11-09 · Realistic test primers and k = 6

**Commit:** `0e0e449`

**Note:** most primers used in real life are 18-30 letters (bases) long:
long enough to stick to only one place in a genome, short enough to stick
quickly. The CDC primers and probes are 18-24 letters.

### What I did
- Noticed my made-up test primers were only 16 letters long, while real qPCR
  primers are 18-30. The 16 had no real reason behind it, so I redid every
  hand-solvable test with new made-up primers of 18, 20, 24 and 30 letters
  and a 26-letter probe, and worked out every answer again **(#38)**.
- A new test shows the same 6-letter deletion is spotted in a 30-letter
  primer but not in an 18-letter one, because too few letters would be left
  to be sure it is not chance **(#38)**.
- Learned what the lookup table's word length (k) does. The program cuts each
  primer into pieces (one more piece than the mismatches allowed), so at least
  one piece must match exactly (the pigeonhole principle), and looks up the
  start of each piece. Every piece must be at least k letters long **(#39)**.
- Changed k from 5 to 6. Longer words match fewer random places, so the
  program is faster (tests: ~18 s down to ~10 s), and all real primers are
  long enough. The CDC and variant results did not change **(#39)**.
- The cost: when a primer fails, the "where did it almost stick" search can
  now miss a site whose mismatches leave no 6-letter stretch intact. A new
  test shows a case that k = 5 finds and k = 6 misses **(#40)**.

---

## Log 8 · 2026-11-09 · 3' risk changes the result; a mislabelled genome

**Commit:** filled in at the next update

### What I did
- Made a bad mismatch at a primer's 3' end count. Before, it was only a
  warning and the product still looked fine. Now such a product is
  **"at risk"**: it may still copy, but worse. A clean product always ranks
  above an at-risk one, and later, on my website, primer pairs that are at
  risk will be flagged and suggested last **(#41)**.
- Looked for a published primer set on the spike gene and found the Yale
  spike 69-70 assay (Vogels et al. 2021). Its probe sits right across Alpha's
  6-letter deletion, so it should fail on Alpha.
- It did not fail on my "Alpha" genome. Checking the spike mutations showed
  why: the file has all of Beta's mutations and none of Alpha's. The wrong
  genome had been saved as Alpha. I renamed it to Beta and flagged the old
  Alpha results as Beta results **(#42)**.
- Omicron BA.1 does have the 69-70 deletion: the spike primers still copy
  the DNA there, but the probe cannot bind, so the test gives no signal.

---

## Where things stand
Still open after version 4 (details at the end of
`modification documentation.md`): a few search limits, and binding is
still yes/no. The first variant run (Log 6) used only one genome per variant.
Next: melting temperature (factor 2); the plan is under "Planned" at the end
of `modification documentation.md`.
----
## Log 8 · 2026-11-09 · 3' risk changes the result; a mislabelled genome

**Commit:** filled in at the next update

**#41. Problem:** a severe mismatch at a primer's 3' end only printed a
warning; the product still counted as a plain "product" (#37), so a pair
likely to amplify poorly looked as good as a perfect one.
**Fix:** new product status **"at risk"**: both primers bind (and the probe,
if given), but a primer site has `three_prime_risk` "high" (a severe mismatch
within `THREE_PRIME_WINDOW` = 3 bases of the 3' end). `product_status`
returns it after the "no signal" and "not assessable" checks. The new
`STATUS_ORDER` = product > at risk > not assessable > no signal > no product
is used by `assay_outcome` and is meant to rank primer pairs on the future
website (at-risk pairs flagged and suggested last). LOW and POSSIBLE risk do
not change the status. The probe's 3' risk is ignored: a TaqMan probe is
never extended. Warnings now cover "at risk" products too;
`cdc_reference_check.py` and `variant_check.py` count "at risk" products as
products. Case 3b now expects "at risk"; new Case 3d (two copies, one with
the severe 3' mismatch) gives two "at risk" products and one "product", and
the assay is "product". Cases 21a/21b check that LOW and POSSIBLE stay
"product". The CDC and variant results do not change (no HIGH 3' risk).

**#42. Problem:** `Alpha_B.1.1.7_MZ068155.fasta` is not Alpha. At the spike
signature positions it carries all of Beta's (B.1.351) changes (D80A
A21801C, D215G, K417N, E484K, N501Y, Δ242-244) and none of Alpha's (ΔH69/V70,
ΔY144, A570D, P681H, T716I). The NCBI record (MZ068155.1,
SARS-CoV-2/human/PHL/COVID53909/2021) names no lineage; the label came from
the file name. Found while testing a spike Δ69-70 assay, which should fail on
Alpha but gave a product on this genome.
**Fix:** renamed with `git mv` to `Beta_B.1.351_MZ068155.fasta`
(`variant_check.py` now labels it "Beta"; its header comment flags the
change). Every "Alpha" result in Log 6 (#33) is a Beta result; flagged there.
Still to do: confirm the lineage with Nextclade, and add a real Alpha genome
for the Δ69-70 positive control.

---

## Still open (known limits after version 4)
- Near-miss and small-gap searches need an exact 6-base stretch (#15, #40).
- Near-miss limits (#16, #17) were tuned on random sequence, not real genomes
  with repeats.
- Severity is a two-level rule (#20); real effects also depend on
  neighbouring bases and positions beyond the 3' window.
- Sites running off the start print negative positions (e.g. -3-48).
- Input is not cleaned of pasted spaces or line breaks.
- The k-mer index is rebuilt on every run; the test suite takes ~10 s.
- The mismatch allowance can only be changed in the code.
- Variants checked with one isolate each (#33).
- No real Alpha (B.1.1.7) genome: the file saved as Alpha was Beta (#42).
- Severity still does not change "binds"; only a HIGH 3' risk changes the
  product status, to "at risk" (#41). Mild mismatches near the 3' end and
  severe ones elsewhere are warnings only.
- Binding is yes/no: a mismatch that still binds (e.g. the Omicron N1 probe,
  #37) may lower efficiency or probe signal and give a later Ct, which the
  model cannot show yet.

## Planned (not built yet)
- **Factor 2: melting temperature (Tm), nearest-neighbor model.** Sum the
  SantaLucia (1998) stack values in `data/thermodynamics/santalucia_1998_nn.tsv`
  (ΔH, ΔS, plus initiation and symmetry terms) and use
  Tm = ΔH / (ΔS + R·ln(C/4)) − 273.15.
  - **Salt correction:** the table is for 1 M NaCl, but
    `primer3_reference_tm.tsv` used 50 mM monovalent, 3 mM Mg²⁺, 0.8 mM dNTP,
    250 nM oligo. Add a monovalent + Mg²⁺ correction (dNTPs bind some Mg²⁺);
    find out which correction Primer3 uses, then match its Tm values as the
    first check.
  - **Mismatch parameters:** the table has only the 10 matched stacks. Add the
    Allawi & SantaLucia (1997–1998) mismatch stack values so Tm can be
    computed on a variant's real site (G·T is mild, C·C or A·A much worse).

## Log 7 · 2026-11-09 · Realistic test primers and k = 6

**Commit:** `0e0e449`

**Note:** most primers used in real life are 18-30 letters (bases) long:
long enough to stick to only one place in a genome, short enough to stick
quickly. The CDC primers and probes are 18-24 letters.

### What I did
- Noticed my made-up test primers were only 16 letters long, while real qPCR
  primers are 18-30. The 16 had no real reason behind it, so I redid every
  hand-solvable test with new made-up primers of 18, 20, 24 and 30 letters
  and a 26-letter probe, and worked out every answer again **(#38)**.
- A new test shows the same 6-letter deletion is spotted in a 30-letter
  primer but not in an 18-letter one, because too few letters would be left
  to be sure it is not chance **(#38)**.
- Learned what the lookup table's word length (k) does. The program cuts each
  primer into pieces (one more piece than the mismatches allowed), so at least
  one piece must match exactly (the pigeonhole principle), and looks up the
  start of each piece. Every piece must be at least k letters long **(#39)**.
- Changed k from 5 to 6. Longer words match fewer random places, so the
  program is faster (tests: ~18 s down to ~10 s), and all real primers are
  long enough. The CDC and variant results did not change **(#39)**.
- The cost: when a primer fails, the "where did it almost stick" search can
  now miss a site whose mismatches leave no 6-letter stretch intact. A new
  test shows a case that k = 5 finds and k = 6 misses **(#40)**.

---

## Log 8 · 2026-11-09 · 3' risk changes the result; a mislabelled genome

**Commit:** filled in at the next update

### What I did
- Made a bad mismatch at a primer's 3' end count. Before, it was only a
  warning and the product still looked fine. Now such a product is
  **"at risk"**: it may still copy, but worse. A clean product always ranks
  above an at-risk one, and later, on my website, primer pairs that are at
  risk will be flagged and suggested last **(#41)**.
- Looked for a published primer set on the spike gene and found the Yale
  spike 69-70 assay (Vogels et al. 2021). Its probe sits right across Alpha's
  6-letter deletion, so it should fail on Alpha.
- It did not fail on my "Alpha" genome. Checking the spike mutations showed
  why: the file has all of Beta's mutations and none of Alpha's. The wrong
  genome had been saved as Alpha. I renamed it to Beta and flagged the old
  Alpha results as Beta results **(#42)**.
- Omicron BA.1 does have the 69-70 deletion: the spike primers still copy
  the DNA there, but the probe cannot bind, so the test gives no signal.

---

## Where things stand
Still open after version 4 (details at the end of
`modification documentation.md`): a few search limits, and binding is
still yes/no. The first variant run (Log 6) used only one genome per variant.
Next: melting temperature (factor 2); the plan is under "Planned" at the end
of `modification documentation.md`.
----
## Log 8 · 2026-11-09 · 3' risk changes the result; a mislabelled genome

**Commit:** filled in at the next update

**#41. Problem:** a severe mismatch at a primer's 3' end only printed a
warning; the product still counted as a plain "product" (#37), so a pair
likely to amplify poorly looked as good as a perfect one.
**Fix:** new product status **"at risk"**: both primers bind (and the probe,
if given), but a primer site has `three_prime_risk` "high" (a severe mismatch
within `THREE_PRIME_WINDOW` = 3 bases of the 3' end). `product_status`
returns it after the "no signal" and "not assessable" checks. The new
`STATUS_ORDER` = product > at risk > not assessable > no signal > no product
is used by `assay_outcome` and is meant to rank primer pairs on the future
website (at-risk pairs flagged and suggested last). LOW and POSSIBLE risk do
not change the status. The probe's 3' risk is ignored: a TaqMan probe is
never extended. Warnings now cover "at risk" products too;
`cdc_reference_check.py` and `variant_check.py` count "at risk" products as
products. Case 3b now expects "at risk"; new Case 3d (two copies, one with
the severe 3' mismatch) gives two "at risk" products and one "product", and
the assay is "product". Cases 21a/21b check that LOW and POSSIBLE stay
"product". The CDC and variant results do not change (no HIGH 3' risk).

signature positions it carries all of Beta's (B.1.351) changes (D80A
A21801C, D215G, K417N, E484K, N501Y, Δ242-244) and none of Alpha's (ΔH69/V70,
ΔY144, A570D, P681H, T716I). The NCBI record (MZ068155.1,
SARS-CoV-2/human/PHL/COVID53909/2021) names no lineage; the label came from
the file name. Found while testing a spike Δ69-70 assay, which should fail on
Alpha but gave a product on this genome.
